INNOVA CAPTAB | JAMMU RAMP-UP + CDMO OPERATING LEVERAGE

CURRENT POSITION
- Market cap: ~₹6,352 Cr | Price: ~₹91 | 1D: +1.5%
- Two-engine business: CDMO + branded/trade generics.
- Q1 FY27 revenue: ₹470.9 Cr, +34% YoY.
- CDMO revenue: ₹328.7 Cr, +32%.
- Branded generics: ₹142.2 Cr, +39%.
- Exports contribute ~32% of revenue.
- 350+ CDMO customers across Baddi, Dehradun, Taloja and Jammu.

BUSINESS & MOAT
- Multi-site capabilities across cephalosporins, beta-lactams, penems, injectables and oral solids/liquids.
- Baddi cephalosporin block has UK-MHRA approval.
- Jammu blocks have PIC/S certification and EU-GMP compliance.
- Customer qualification and plant audits create switching costs.
- 14 of 15 existing Jammu customers had completed audits or were expected to start business around Q4 FY26/Q1 FY27.
- CDMO contracts use cost-plus pricing, allowing raw-material/API price changes to be passed through, although with a timing lag.
- Sharon acquisition adds regulated-market exposure across Canada, UK, Europe and Australia.

MARGIN INFLECTION
- FY26 EBITDA margin: 15.4% | EBITDA: ₹250.3 Cr.
- Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin: 16% | EBITDA: ₹75.1 Cr.
- Core business excluding Jammu operates at ~20% EBITDA margin.
- Jammu currently suppresses consolidated margins because of depreciation and underutilisation.
- As Jammu utilisation rises, fixed-cost absorption should drive EBITDA growth faster than revenue.
- Management highlighted potential for normalized margins of ~17–18%.

JAMMU — KEY GROWTH ENGINE
- Q1 FY27 Jammu revenue: ₹107 Cr vs ₹90 Cr in the previous quarter.
- Current utilisation only ~25–30%.
- Peak revenue potential: ~₹1,400 Cr at 65–70% utilisation.
- Current annualised revenue run-rate is only ~₹428 Cr.
- If ramp-up continues, Jammu could reach ~50–60% utilisation over 18–24 months.
- Potential Jammu revenue at that level: ~₹800–1,000 Cr.
- Jammu became EBITDA positive in Q1 FY27 at ~₹1–1.5 Cr.
- PAT breakeven is now expected during FY27.

NEW Baddi CAPACITY
- ₹150–170 Cr capex planned across FY27–FY28 for a new general oral block.
- Potential revenue at optimum utilisation: ~₹450–500 Cr.
- Commercial production expected around FY28.
- This provides a second capacity-led growth driver beyond Jammu.

GROWTH & EARNINGS PATH
- FY27 management target: 20%+ overall growth.
- FY27 revenue could reach ~₹1,950 Cr based on ~20% growth over FY26 revenue of ~₹1,630 Cr.
- At 15–16% EBITDA margin, FY27 EBITDA could be ~₹292–312 Cr.
- Jammu operating leverage should allow EBITDA growth to outpace revenue.
- With depreciation and interest largely fixed, PAT growth could reach high-20s to 30% range.
- Over 18–24 months, the thesis points toward 20%+ revenue growth with EBITDA margin moving toward ~17–18%.

MANAGEMENT WALK-TALK
- FY26 Jammu revenue target was initially ~₹400 Cr, later revised to ₹270–280 Cr.
- Company delivered the revised target.
- FY27 20%+ growth commitment was followed by Q1 FY27 revenue growth of 34%.
- Jammu EBITDA-positive milestone for Q1 FY27 was achieved.
- PAT breakeven guidance was pushed from FY26 to FY27, showing some execution slippage.
- Overall pattern: management has revised aggressive expectations when required, but has generally delivered against the revised targets.

CAPITAL ALLOCATION
- Maintenance capex: ~₹20–25 Cr annually.
- Growth capex: ~₹20–30 Cr annually in addition to the Baddi expansion.
- Baddi oral block capex: ₹150–170 Cr over two years.
- No indication of a dilutive equity raise.
- Operating cash generation is expected to support planned expansion.

KEY RISKS / FALSIFIERS
- Jammu utilisation is the single most important monitorable.
- Customer onboarding, stability data and ROW regulatory approvals could delay the ramp-up.
- API price volatility remains a risk despite cost-plus contracts because of the pass-through lag.
- If Jammu remains stuck at low utilisation, expected operating leverage and margin expansion will be delayed.
- Semaglutide and new regulated-market opportunities provide optionality but timelines remain less certain.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Jammu ramp-up + Baddi expansion could drive 20%+ growth and lift margins toward 17–18%.

ANTHEM BIOSCIENCES | CRDMO SCALE-UP + COMMERCIALIZATION INFLECTION

CURRENT POSITION
- Market cap: ~₹52,871 Cr | Price: ~₹87 | 1D: +1.7%
- Q1 FY27 revenue declined 22.6% and PAT declined 12%, but management highlighted ~60% order-book visibility and added a new large pharma client.
- Business mix: ~81.5% contract work and ~18.5% proprietary B2B products.
- Focused on CRDMO, complex chemistry, APIs, peptides, fermentation and newer modalities rather than commodity-volume manufacturing.

WHY THE BUSINESS HAS A MOAT
- High customer switching costs once Anthem's discovery and development work becomes embedded in a client's clinical pipeline.
- Regulatory qualification and technical integration make switching CDMO partners difficult and risky.
- Capabilities across ADCs, oligonucleotides, peptides, APIs and fermentation broaden the addressable opportunity.
- Backward integration improves economics by converting commodity inputs into specialized products.
- In-house fermentation fragments for GLP-1 peptides and reduced China dependence on selected intermediates supported gross margins above 65% in H2 FY26.

MARGIN QUALITY
- Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin: 39.6%.
- FY26 EBITDA margin: 43.4%.
- FY26 EBITDA: ~₹990 Cr.
- Margins are substantially above typical manufacturing economics, reflecting specialized capabilities, pricing power, yield improvement and backward integration.
- Q1 FY27 revenue weakness was partly linked to deferred deliveries, while margins improved through better yields.

18–24 MONTH GROWTH INFLECTION
- Unit 4 Phase 1 targeted for commissioning by FY28-end.
- Adds ~365 KL custom synthesis capacity + 100 KL fermentation capacity.
- Planned Unit 4 capex: ~₹1,200 Cr across FY27–FY28.
- New capacity could effectively double the existing base.
- 10 Phase 3 molecules, including ADCs, are progressing toward commercialization.
- Four molecules commercialized in FY26 already contribute ~8–9% of revenue and can scale further.
- GLP-1 opportunity is progressing, with CDSCO approval expected within 1–2 quarters according to the thesis.
- Biosimilar asset is expected to start contributing to P&L from FY27.
- Neo Anthem is expected to move toward break-even/profitability in FY27.

ORDER BOOK & UTILISATION
- ~60% order-book visibility provides some near-term revenue visibility despite Q1 softness.
- Key earnings driver is higher utilisation across Units 1, 2 and 3.
- Unit 4 must secure sufficient order intake to support the targeted ~1.4–1.5x asset-turn ratio.
- Commercialisation of late-phase molecules could shift the revenue mix toward higher-volume commercial manufacturing.

MANAGEMENT WALK-TALK
- Nov 2025: guided toward upper end of 36–37% EBITDA margin and targeted Unit 3 fermentation commissioning by FY26-end.
- Feb 2026: 9M EBITDA margin reached 41.5%, exceeding guidance; Unit 2 expansion completed.
- May 2026: Unit 4 Phase 1 timeline maintained for March 2028.
- FY26 EBITDA reached ₹990 Cr at 43.4% margin.
- Management has historically targeted ~20% growth across revenue, EBITDA and PAT, although FY27 was not given with explicit numerical guidance.

BALANCE SHEET / CAPEX
- Net cash: ~₹1,720 Cr as of June 30, 2026.
- Strong balance sheet allows the ₹1,200 Cr Unit 4 investment to be funded internally.
- No dilution expected for the planned Unit 4 capex.

KEY RISKS / FALSIFIERS
- Unit 4 execution and commissioning remain the biggest operational monitorable.
- Late-phase molecules must successfully transition into commercial supply.
- Unit 4 needs adequate order intake to achieve targeted asset turns.
- Clinical outcomes for the late-stage pipeline remain an important uncertainty.
- Q1 revenue decline shows that delivery timing can create quarterly volatility even when underlying margins remain strong.
- If commercialisation or capacity ramp-up gets delayed, the expected earnings acceleration could shift out.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Unit 4 + late-phase commercialization + GLP-1/ADC pipeline could sustain Anthem's high-margin CRDMO growth.

SHIVALIK BIMETAL CONTROLS | PRECISION MATERIALS + EV & SMART METER GROWTH

CURRENT POSITION
- Stock gained 10% in 1D to around ₹98.
- No major announcement identified behind the move.
- Market cap ~₹6,279 Cr.
- FY26 revenue: ₹570.9 Cr.
- Existing asset base can support revenue of up to ~₹1,300 Cr.
- Current utilisation ~60%, with management targeting ~75% in FY27.

BUSINESS & MARKET POSITION
- Manufactures thermostatic bimetals, EB-welded shunt resistors and silver electrical contacts.
- New Pune facility adds Cell Connecting Systems (CCS), busbars and PCBA assemblies.
- Management estimates ~90% share of India's switchgear bimetal segment.
- Global bimetal market is concentrated, with 4–5 large players accounting for ~70–80% of volumes.
- Very few global suppliers can manufacture its specific EB-welded shunt products.
- No known Indian competitor currently performs the same EB welding or manufactures these busbar assemblies domestically.

HIGH ENTRY & SWITCHING BARRIERS
- EB-welding know-how has been developed over 30+ years.
- Development-to-commercialisation typically takes 18–24 months.
- Customer ramp-up can take another 4–5 years, with first-year volumes only ~10–20% of forecast.
- Alternate supplier qualification is difficult, costly and time-consuming.
- No major Indian switchgear manufacturer is reportedly outside Shivalik's customer base.
- These qualification barriers helped protect existing business even during the 50% US tariff environment.

MARGIN & VALUE-ADDED SHIFT
- FY26 EBITDA margin expanded ~250 bps to 22.9%.
- Q3 FY26 EBITDA margin exceeded 24%.
- Q1 FY27 EBITDA stood at ₹43.2 Cr on ₹182.2 Cr revenue, ~23.7% margin.
- Q1 FY27 PAT grew 44.9% YoY.
- Finished shunt components generate 10–12% higher realisation per kg versus strip.
- Average shunt realisation increased to ~₹3,290/kg from ~₹2,000/kg in FY23.
- Component share of shunt supply reached ~65% in FY26.
- Management attributes 70–75% of shunt growth to value-added conversion rather than material-price inflation.

PUNE FACILITY — NEXT GROWTH ENGINE
- Phase 1 received consent to operate after Q1 FY27 and currently supports one 2-wheeler OEM model.
- Main Pune facility is expected to become fully operational in October 2026.
- Total project capex is only ~₹20–25 Cr because expensive welding capacity already exists at Solan.
- Assembly revenue targeted at 15–16% of total revenue in the first year.
- Management targets ₹150–200 Cr assembly revenue in year two and ₹300+ Cr by year three.
- 2–3 additional CCS designs are expected to convert by end-CY26.
- December 2026 quarter is therefore a key thesis checkpoint.

SMART METERS & SHUNT RECOVERY
- Smart-meter revenue more than doubled to >₹75–80 Cr in FY26.
- Management expects smart-meter revenue to double again in FY27.
- Momentum could continue for 6–8 quarters.
- Largest US resistor customer is expected to return to peak revenue in FY27 and exceed it in FY28.
- Incremental US volume is expected to be in component form, providing nearly double the value-add versus strip.

FY27 GROWTH POTENTIAL
- Management's FY27 growth expectation has increased from 13–18% in late 2025 to 20–30% by Aug 2026.
- FY26 revenue of ₹570.9 Cr implies FY27 revenue of roughly ₹685–745 Cr at 20–30% growth.
- At 23–25% EBITDA margin, potential FY27 EBITDA is ~₹160–185 Cr.
- Q1 FY27 PAT growth of 44.9% indicates strong earnings flow-through already.
- Consolidated margins are expected to remain around 23–25% despite lower-margin assembly contribution.

CAPITAL ALLOCATION
- Expansion is being funded internally.
- Maintenance capex remains low at ~₹10–15 Cr annually.
- Working-capital days of ~250–260 are being targeted toward <180–200 days.
- Domestic raw-material sourcing should support working-capital improvement.
- Customer concentration has reduced from historical 38–39% to ~13–14%.
- Management intends to keep concentration below ~17–18%.

WALK-TALK RECORD
- FY26 growth guidance was cut from 12–15% to high-single digits in Nov 2025 due to US tariffs.
- Final FY26 growth of 12.3% remained within the original guidance range.
- Domestic bimetal recovery of 15–20% did not materialise; Indian bimetal remained largely flat due to weak switchgear and housing demand.
- Margin delivery was stronger than guidance, with Q3 FY26 EBITDA margin exceeding 24%.
- Pune commissioning was delayed from the earlier March/April timeline to full operation in October 2026.
- Despite the delay, FY27 growth guidance has been raised to 20–30%.

KEY RISKS / FALSIFIERS
- Main Pune facility must operate at scale from October 2026.
- 2–3 pending CCS designs must convert by end-CY26.
- Indian 2-wheeler EV volumes remain important, but OEM forecasts can be unreliable.
- The December 2026 quarter is the biggest near-term monitorable.
- If busbar/CCS revenue does not ramp after commissioning, the ₹150–200 Cr year-two assembly target becomes questionable.
- Indian bimetal recovery remains a weaker area.
- Q1 growth was partly helped by higher silver prices, creating a need to distinguish commodity inflation from structural growth.
- Strip sales fell to one-third of the prior-year level, making the value-added mix shift particularly important to monitor.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- Pune CCS ramp-up + smart meters + shunt component conversion could drive 20–30% growth while sustaining 23–25% EBITDA margins.

Supriya Lifescience - FY26 Annual Report Analysis

Supriya Lifescience is a niche pharmaceutical company engaged in developing & manufacturing Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API), finished dosage formulations & CMO/CDMO solutions. The company supplies more than 40 specialised APIs to over 1,500 customers across 120+ countries.

The company has historically operated as an API manufacturer but is gradually evolving into an integrated life sciences platform. Its next phase involves expanding into finished formulations, developing new niche APIs & undertaking long term contract manufacturing programmes for global pharmaceutical & innovator companies.

The business is highly export oriented, with international markets contributing 82% of FY26 REV. Europe is the largest geography with a 40% share, followed by Asia at 33%, Latin America at 20%, North America at 3% & other markets at 4%.

Backward integration is central to Supriya’s business model. Backward integrated products contributed 76% of FY26 REV.

The model also gives Supriya greater flexibility while negotiating long term contracts with global customers. Customers in regulated markets value consistency, traceability & supply security alongside pricing, making backward integration an important competitive advantage.

Supriya has a portfolio of more than 40 APIs, including 15 backward integrated products. Its major therapeutic categories include anaesthetics, antihistamines, analgesics, vitamins, anti-asthmatics, anti-allergics, antihypertensives & other specialised products.

Anaesthetics are the largest therapeutic category, contributing 54% of REV. Management is addressing this by launching products across cardiovascular, ADHD, liquid anaesthetics & other niche therapeutic segments.

Newer products started contributing meaningfully during FY26. A cardiovascular product launched during Q3FY26 has begun scaling with a strong order pipeline, while the ADHD portfolio witnessed encouraging demand across Europe & Latin America.

The company also commercialised a liquid anaesthetic API & began regular supplies during the year. Four new APIs were successfully developed & commercialised. Management intends to commercialise three to four new products annually.

CMO/CDMO is emerging as an important long term growth engine. Instead of manufacturing only its own APIs, Supriya is increasingly working with pharmaceutical companies to develop & manufacture products under dedicated or exclusive arrangements.

The company is evaluating exclusive manufacturing opportunities in liquid inhalation products, GLP-1 development & supply for an Indian generics company. Multiple finished dosage development & supply opportunities are also under consideration.

Supriya is expanding beyond APIs into finished dosage formulations through its Ambernath facility. The formulation platform is developing products across tablets, capsules, injections, nasal sprays and liquid inhalation products.

The company commissioned a dedicated production block for a CMO customer & installed a precision distillation facility for a strategic API supporting long term contract manufacturing opportunities.

Planning has commenced for two additional manufacturing blocks at Lote. These investments will support new products, higher volumes & additional CMO/CDMO opportunities.

The Ambernath facility expands Supriya’s capabilities beyond APIs into formulation development & manufacturing. The company is also developing a new industrial site at Isambe, Patalganga, which can provide capacity for the next phase of growth.

Supriya operates three R&D centres - two focused on APIs & one on formulations. It employs around 90 scientists across API & formulation process development.

Supriya is increasing its participation in regulated markets such as Europe, the US & Japan. The unannounced USFDA inspection of the Lote facility in February 2026 concluded with one minor observation, which was subsequently addressed. 🏛️ Ministry of Information & Broadcasting has proposed a 20% ceiling on cross-holdings across television channels, DTH and Headend-in-the-Sky (HITS) services under the draft Telecommunications (Television, Radio and Allied Services) Rules, 2026.

📊 Under the proposal, a TV channel entity, alone or together with an MSO, cannot hold more than 20% in a DTH entity; similarly, a DTH entity cannot hold more than 20% in a TV channel entity or MSO.

🏦 Financial institutional investors are proposed to be exempt from these cross-holding restrictions.

🔐 Any ownership/control change resulting in change of control or complete management change would require prior written approval from the Central Government.

📝 Changes in shareholding/FDI would need to be reported within 30 days, while certain ownership/control and other material changes must be reported within 15 days.

⏳ Proposed authorisation periods:

TV channels, teleports & community radio: 10 years

DTH & HITS: 20 years

Private radio: 15 years

⚠️ Renewal would be linked to regulatory compliance and security clearance; the draft says private radio services would not be eligible for renewal under the proposed framework.

📑 The draft aims to consolidate six existing broadcasting frameworks, covering satellite TV uplinking/downlinking, DTH, HITS, private FM, community radio and IPTV.

⚠️ Important: These are draft proposals under public consultation and are not yet effective.

🟡 Impact: Mixed/Negative for integrated broadcasting groups — a 20% cross-holding cap could restrict common ownership structures and future consolidation across TV, DTH and HITS, while increasing compliance requirements. Peptides are quietly becoming one of the biggest manufacturing opportunities in pharma.

Most people know peptides because of Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. But the bigger story is what is happening behind these drugs.

So, what exactly is a peptide?

A peptide is simply a chain of amino acids — think of amino acids as molecular beads joined together in a specific sequence. Insulin is a peptide. Semaglutide has 31 amino acids and tirzepatide has 39. Unlike conventional small-molecule drugs, these are larger, more complex molecules that require a very different manufacturing process.

Why are peptides suddenly so important?

Because pharma has moved beyond using peptides mainly for relatively niche diseases. GLP-1 drugs have demonstrated that peptide medicines can address massive patient populations, particularly obesity, diabetes and metabolic diseases. The result is a specialist chemistry becoming an industrial-scale manufacturing opportunity.

And this is where the investment opportunity gets interesting.

The peptide value chain is much longer than a conventional API value chain.

It starts with amino acids, the basic building blocks. These are converted into protected amino acids and resins, which are the actual consumables used in peptide synthesis. Companies can then make peptide fragments — short pre-built pieces of the final molecule — before moving into chain assembly.

The peptide is then purified, isolated and converted into the final peptide API. From there, another set of capabilities is required for sterile fill-finish, followed increasingly by cartridge, syringe and injection-pen assembly.

So the chain looks roughly like:

Amino acids → Protected amino acids → Resins → Fragments → Peptide synthesis → Purification → API → Sterile fill-finish → Pen/device

And the economics change dramatically as you move up and down this chain.

Here is the part I find particularly interesting.

Peptide synthesis is not simply “put chemicals into a reactor and make the API.”

In solid-phase peptide synthesis, the molecule is built one amino acid at a time on tiny resin beads. Add one amino acid. Wash. Remove the protecting group. Wash. Add the next amino acid. Wash. Repeat.

For a 31-amino-acid peptide, this cycle is repeated dozens of times, and every individual step has to work extremely well because small errors accumulate as the chain becomes longer.

But synthesis is only half the problem.

After synthesis, you don't have a clean bucket of the desired peptide. You have the desired molecule mixed with many extremely similar impurities — peptides that may have missed an amino acid, picked up an unwanted reaction product or developed other structural impurities.

That is why purification is such a critical bottleneck.

Large chromatography systems, solvent handling, isolation and lyophilisation are required to turn the crude peptide into pharmaceutical-grade API. In many cases, purification can take longer than synthesis itself.

The numbers explain why this matters.

Raw materials can represent roughly 60–70% of peptide production cost. Solid-phase manufacturing can also generate enormous quantities of waste, while a large commercial peptide facility can require hundreds of millions of dollars of investment.

This creates several different ways for Indian pharma companies to win.

DivisLaboratories is moving backwards into the value chain — manufacturing peptide building blocks, protected amino acids and fragments itself. The logic is powerful: if raw materials are such a large part of the cost, owning the building blocks can turn a cost into a source of margin and reduce dependence on external suppliers.

NeulandLaboratories is taking a different route. It is investing heavily in peptide synthesis capacity and focusing on complex peptides for innovators rather than simply chasing commodity GLP-1 volumes. In other words: compete on complexity, not volume.

LaurusLabs is building across peptide synthesis, purification and isolation, with significant capex being directed towards peptides and other new modalities. The ambition is to make CDMO a much larger part of the overall business.

SaiLifeSciences is taking the “follow the molecule” approach — starting with discovery and development and trying to stay with the customer as the molecule progresses towards commercialisation. Its peptide strategy also includes fragments, which can be an attractive entry point without immediately building the entire commercial peptide chain.

Then there is the last mile.

OneSourceSpecialtyPharma is positioned much further downstream, around sterile fill-finish and drug-device combinations. This is important because the patient doesn't receive a drum of peptide API. The patient receives a vial, cartridge, pre-filled syringe or injection pen.

That makes the drug-device interface another potential bottleneck — particularly for GLP-1 therapies. OneSource's expansion in drug-device combination capacity and its large GLP-1 customer base demonstrate how value can migrate downstream in the chain.

Biocon brings another interesting advantage: decades of insulin experience, which is directly relevant because insulin itself is a peptide. It is building GLP-1 injectable capabilities across vials, cartridges, pre-filled syringes and devices.

GlandPharma brings large-scale sterile injectable manufacturing.

ShilpaMedicare is extending its oncology API base into peptides.

BlueJetHealthcare is entering through peptide building blocks.

And GranulesIndia has entered the space through the acquisition of Swiss peptide CDMO Senn Chemicals.

A company with a peptide laboratory is not the same as a company with commercial peptide manufacturing.

A company with synthesis capacity is not the same as one with purification capacity.

And having peptide API capability is not the same as controlling the final drug-device bottleneck.

The most interesting companies may ultimately be those that occupy a narrow, difficult-to-replicate bottleneck rather than those that simply claim to have “peptide capabilities.”

Don't just track who is entering peptides. Track which rung of the ladder they are climbing — and where the bottleneck sits.

Because in CDMO, the value rarely goes to whoever has the loudest narrative. It goes to whoever controls the hardest step to replicate.

Is Pvt Banks Really Losing Share vs PSU Banks?

Everyone is talking about PSU banks taking share from Pvt banks. The narrative is simple: PSU banks are growing faster than Pvt banks, so PSU banks are winning. But the reality is a lot more nuanced.

Argument is : PSU banks are fine with 1.0-1.3% RoA vs  Pvt banks target higher profitability. Pvt banks don't want to trade-off profitability for growth.

This has impacted valuations. Premium Pvt bank multiples came with expectation of steadily MS gain vs PSU. Post-Covid, that trend has slowed, creating doubts.

If PSU banks are sacrificing yield for growth, where should it show up first? HFC, safest retail assets with low NPA, Yet PSU bank share has drifted from ~35% in FY21 to ~34% in H1FY26, while Pvt banks have inched up from ~39% to ~40%.

If PSU banks were aggressively chasing growth regardless of return, housing should have been the biggest battleground. The data doesn't show that. PSU gained initially, now plateaued. 

PSU not gainin share from Pvt banks. Market share remained stable, data also inc. HDFC merger boost for pvt bank

So where is PSU growth actually coming from? A large part is Gold Loans.

Many Pvt banks have stayed away from becoming aggressive gold lenders. The business is operationally intensive and risky. PSU banks have been far more active, esp Canara/SBIN. 

Recently, incremental industry gold loan growth has come primarily from PSU banks, increasing their dominance in banking gold-loan AUM.

🇮🇳 India’s $4 TRILLION gold 🧈🧈🧈 wealth effect may be one of the most underappreciated macro stories. 

Indian households own 25,000 tonnes of gold — worth $3.9 trillion, 𝙪𝙥 𝙖𝙣 𝙚𝙭𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙤𝙧𝙙𝙞𝙣𝙖𝙧𝙮 ~$2 𝙩𝙧𝙞𝙡𝙡𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙞𝙣 𝙟𝙪𝙨𝙩 2 𝙮𝙚𝙖𝙧𝙨

That means that the value of gold held by Indians is almost 100% of GDP

Some striking numbers:

 🌕 Gold is now ~24% of household wealth, versus just ~6% in equities

🏦 Household gold is worth ~2x bank deposits and ~4x equities

💰 Organised gold loans have surged from $86bn → $197bn in 3 years, a ~32% CAGR

📈 Yet gold loans are only 5.1% of household gold value, below 5.9% two years ago — gold prices have risen faster than monetisation

💳 Including informal lending, only ~15% of household gold may currently be monetised

📊 Gold ETF AUM has exploded from $2.8bn in Mar-23 → $18.5bn in Mar-26

Unlike equities, gold ownership extends deep into rural and lower-income India. Rising gold prices therefore create a potentially broader wealth effect.

If monetisation catches up, Jefferies estimates gold loans could rise another $15–20bn annually. And every further 10% rise in gold creates roughly $400bn of household wealth and potentially $20–25bn of additional gold loans.

That could translate into a  spending tailwind of 0.8% to 1% of GDP.

⚠️ But there is another side: India imported $79bn of gold in FY26 (~2% of GDP) versus $36bn in FY23. What strengthens household balance sheets can simultaneously worsen the current account.

Gold is therefore becoming more than a store of wealth in India — it is increasingly a transmission mechanism from global gold prices → household collateral → credit → consumption.

Source: Jefferies

Many Problem: Solar led grid instability / Energy import / Pollution One solution: EV India is winning solar race. Solar supply a huge chunk of daytime power, pushing net grid demand sharply lower arnd noon. But demand peaks after sunset. That's the classic "duck curve" problem

~80 GW swing created largely by renewable output. The irony: clean power is available when demand isn't. Several states doing solar curtailment as the grid couldn't absorb all midday generation. So, next phase of green transition is tougher than just adding more solar panels

India imports ~90% of its crude oil needs & roughly half of its natural gas . Energy security remains one of the biggest economic vulnerabilities. Crude oil is among India's largest import items. Every $ oil prices widens the import bill = trade deficit = pressure on Rupee

Air pollution remains a public health emergency in major metros. Delhi frequently records PM2.5 levels many multiples above WHO norms, while Mumbai too has seen worsening air quality episodes. Solar, oil imports & air pollution are not separate challenges. They are connected

The common link is urban transport. A large share of oil consumption in metros comes from ICE cars commuting daily between home & office. Think about office parking lots. Vehicles remain parked for 8-10 hrs during the exact period when solar generation is highest

What if every major office complex became a daytime EV charging hub? Cars would consume power when solar generation is abundant, helping flatten the duck curve instead of deepening it.

Corp can accelerate this shift. EV subsidy for employees & workplace chargin infra can become part of CSR spend (2% of PBT) Vehicles in metros spend most working hours parked at offices. Converting 20%+ of parking capacity into chargers can create a daytime demand for solar power

One solution. Multiple benefits. More EVs = lower oil imports, cleaner city air, higher daytime power consumption, better solar utilisation & stable grid. Sometimes the smartest energy storage isn't a battery plant. It's millions of parked EVs connected to chargers.

Underappreciated SBI MF's distribution moat 

SBI MF's biggest advantage isn't fund performance. It's distribution. In India, bank-backed AMCs blessed with an edge as the bank branch is still the most powerful financial distribution channel
Investors trust banks with savings, salaries & FDs. Convincing a depositor to buy a bank-sponsored MF is far easier than acquiring a customer from scratch. Trust compounds over time
This trust factor is visible across the industry. 4 of India's top 5 AMCs are bank-backed. Even with rising competition, large AMCs have largely retained market share
SBI has the widest reach across the country, with one of the largest branch networks, customer bases & geographic presence among all financial institutions. That reach is difficult to replicate
Unlike most AMCs, SBI MF gets disproportionate support from its parent. SBI Bank contributes 35% of SBI MF's equity AUM. Compare that with just 8% for ICICI AMC & 6% for HDFC AMC
More interestingly, 40% of SBI MF's equity AUM comes through bank channels, versus 19% for ICICI AMC & 12% for HDFC AMC. SBI's distribution engine remains a major growth driver
Most banks operate open architecture & recommend products across AMCs based on suitability. SBI may have open architecture formally, but data suggests SBI customers get mostly SBI-branded investment products
The numbers are striking. 100% of SBI MF's promoter-bank sourced AUM sits with SBI, vs 70% for ICICI AMC & just 28% for HDFC AMC. That's about as captive as distribution gets
SBI's MF penetration opportunity is still huge. Average MF AUM per SBI branch is only ~10% of retail deposits per branch, implying a long runway for existing customers to migrate from deposits into MFs

The Relationship Trump Misunderstood:
For three decades, China and emerging markets effectively exported disinflation to the developed world. They produced goods at a fraction of Western costs and shipped them to consumers in the US and Europe. The result: lower prices and higher purchasing power
The West got cheaper TVs, phones, clothes, furniture and industrial goods. China got manufacturing jobs, export growth and rising incomes. It wasn't a one-way relationship. Both sides benefited
As exports surged, China accumulated enormous foreign exchange reserves. Every dollar earned from exports added to a growing pool of savings that had to be invested somewhere
Those reserves served two purposes: protect the yuan from volatility and build strategic national wealth. China used them to buy foreign assets, resources, companies and financial securities around the world
A large portion of those reserves found their way into US Treasuries. China became one of the largest lenders to the US government, recycling export earnings back into America's financial system
This mattered because sustained Treasury demand helped keep long-term US interest rates lower than they otherwise would have been. Cheap imports lowered inflation. Treasury purchases lowered financing costs
In effect, China was helping on two fronts: suppressing goods inflation through low-cost manufacturing and supporting bond markets through reserve recycling. 
Trump focused heavily on one side of the equation: the trade deficit. From that perspective, China was exporting too much and manufacturing jobs were leaving America. This became the basis for tariffs and trade confrontation.
But the other side received less attention. Those same imports were keeping prices low for US consumers. Many products became affordable precisely because they were manufactured in lower-cost economies
The relationship also extended to capital markets. China's reserve accumulation created a steady source of demand for US government bonds, helping support the broader financial system
Today that world is changing. China is no longer a low-income economy desperate for export growth. Wages have risen, technology has improved and its economic influence is far greater than it was 20 years ago
The old model of unlimited cheap labour, ever-rising globalization and automatic reserve recycling is fading. Both countries increasingly view the relationship through a strategic lens rather than purely an economic one
As supply chains fragment and tariffs rise, the US may face more inflation from its own policy choices. Producing goods domestically or through alternative supply chains is often more resilient, but rarely cheaper
At the same time, if foreign demand for Treasuries becomes less predictable, bond investors may demand higher yields to absorb increasing government debt. Higher yields mean higher financing costs across the economy
The next decade may look very different from the last three. Less globalization, more strategic competition, potentially higher inflation and structurally higher interest rates. Markets are still figuring out what that world looks like
Bottom line: The US-China relationship wasn't simply buyer vs seller. It was a system where goods, capital and inflation dynamics were deeply intertwined. Breaking that system may create consequences on both sides.
